title: The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3
summary: Documents how the Internet community standardizes protocols and procedures. It defines the maturity stages, what is needed to move a document between them, and the kinds of documents used. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook for how a new idea becomes an official internet rule. It says what tests and approvals it must pass.

questions: how does an rfc become an internet standard
what are the internet standards track stages
what is a last call in the ietf
what is the difference between proposed standard and draft standard
subtitle: The rulebook for how an idea becomes an Internet Standard, from Proposed Standard to full Standard.

tldr.problem: The Internet is run by many independent networks that need common protocols, so the community needs a fair, open and predictable way to decide which specifications become standards.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2026 defines document types, three standards-track maturity levels (Proposed, Draft, Internet Standard), off-track levels, minimum waiting times, IESG review with a Last-Call, an appeals chain, and intellectual property rules.
tldr.outcome: It is published as Best Current Practice 9 and has been updated by many later RFCs, so it is the base document rather than the final word on today's process.

facts.label: Min. Last-Call
facts.value: 2 weeks (4 if not from a working group)

today: RFC 2026 is a Best Current Practice, and later RFCs have updated it, including RFC 6410 and RFC 9282. Read those alongside it, since details in this explainer may have been changed by them.

sections.title: What the Process Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2026 documents the process the Internet community uses to standardize protocols and procedures. The process is an activity of the Internet Society, run on behalf of the community by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG).

The memo says an Internet Standard is stable and well understood, technically competent, has multiple independent and interoperable implementations with substantial operational experience, enjoys significant public support, and is recognizably useful. The stated goals are technical excellence, prior implementation and testing, clear documentation, openness and fairness, and timeliness.

The process deliberately balances two conflicting goals: thorough testing and review take time, but networking technology moves fast.
sections.eli5: Imagine a club that makes rules for how computers talk. Before a rule counts, it has to be fair, tested, and agreed on by lots of people.

sections.title: Documents: RFCs, Drafts and Specifications
sections.content:
Each version of a standards-related specification is published in the Request for Comments (RFC) series, which began in 1969 and is the official publication channel. RFCs that document Internet Standards also get an STD label, and those that document best current practice get a BCP label, but they keep their RFC number.

While work is in progress, drafts live as Internet-Drafts. These have no formal status, can change or vanish at any time, and are removed if unchanged for more than six months without an IESG recommendation. The memo says nobody should reference an Internet-Draft in a paper, report or request for proposal, or claim compliance with one.

Standards-track specifications come in two kinds. A Technical Specification (TS) describes a protocol, service, procedure, convention or format. An Applicability Statement (AS) says how and when one or more TSs apply, and gives each a requirement level: Required, Recommended or Elective. Two more levels, Limited Use and Not Recommended, cover documents that are off the standards track. An AS may not have a higher maturity level than a TS it relies on.
sections.eli5: A draft is a rough sketch that anyone can change. An RFC is the finished, numbered page that goes in the official library.

sections.title: The Maturity Levels
sections.content:
Specifications meant to become standards move through three maturity levels on the standards track.

  • Proposed Standard is the entry level. It is generally stable and has had significant review, but implementers should treat it as immature, and deploying it in a disruption-sensitive environment is not recommended. Implementation experience is usually not required.
  • Draft Standard requires at least two independent and interoperable implementations from different code bases, with sufficient operational experience. This applies to all options and features, and any option not shown in two implementations must be removed before advancing.
  • Internet Standard requires significant implementation and successful operational experience. It is assigned an STD number and keeps its RFC number.

Off the track are three labels: Experimental (research or development efforts), Informational (published for general information, not a community recommendation) and Historic (superseded or otherwise considered obsolete).
sections.eli5: It is like a video game with three levels. Each level needs better proof that the rule really works, and the last one means it is truly dependable.

sections.title: How a Standards Action Proceeds
sections.content:
Any standards action, meaning entering, advancing or removing a specification from the track, must be approved by the IESG. A specification first appears as an Internet-Draft for at least two weeks. The responsible working group then recommends action to its Area Director, or an individual recommends it to the IESG if there is no working group.

The IESG checks the criteria and the technical quality, may commission an independent review, and issues a Last-Call on the IETF Announce mailing list. Anyone may comment. The Last-Call lasts at least two weeks, or at least four weeks if the action did not come from a working group. After approval, the RFC Editor is told to publish.

Minimum times apply: at least six months at Proposed Standard, and at least four months at Draft Standard or until one IETF meeting has occurred, whichever is later. If a specification stays at one level for twenty-four months, the IESG reviews it, then every twelve months, and may keep it or move it to Historic. A new version of an established standard goes through the full process, and a standard can be retired by moving it to Historic.
sections.eli5: First the idea is posted for everyone to read. Then the group in charge asks for last comments, and only after waiting at least a couple of weeks can it be approved.

sections.title: Best Current Practice, Appeals and Variances
sections.content:
The BCP subseries records community consensus on practices and principles rather than protocols. It follows similar review, including a Last-Call, but once the IESG approves, the process ends and the document is published. RFC 2026 itself is a BCP.

Disputes follow a chain. A person first discusses a working group decision with the chairs, then the Area Director, then appeals to the IESG, and then to the IAB, whose decision is final on whether procedures were followed and on technical merit. Complaints about IESG actions go to the IESG Chair, then the IESG, then the IAB. Claims that the procedures themselves are inadequate go to the Internet Society Board of Trustees, whose decision is final. Appeals must start within two months of the action becoming public.

A one-time variance can excuse some requirements if the IESG decides the benefits outweigh the costs, but it needs an extended Last-Call of at least four weeks and cannot lower any specified delays or waive openness, fairness or consensus.
sections.eli5: If someone thinks a decision is wrong, they can ask the next person up the ladder. The ladder has a few steps, and the top step has the last word.

sections.title: External Specifications and Open Records
sections.content:
Many standards come from other bodies such as ANSI, ISO, IEEE and ITU-T. The Internet community will not standardize a mere Internet version of an existing external specification unless an explicit cooperative arrangement exists. An Internet Standard may incorporate an open external standard by reference, and a proprietary specification may be incorporated if its owner meets the memo's intellectual property rules. A working group may also start from an external specification if change control is conveyed to the IETF.

The organizations involved (the IETF, IESG, IAB, working groups and the Internet Society Board of Trustees) must publicly announce and keep public records of their standards activity. Records include charters, minutes, mailing list archives and written contributions, with the IETF Secretariat keeping the formal record.
sections.eli5: When someone else already made a good rule, the club uses theirs instead of making a copy. And everything the club does is written down where anyone can look.

sections.title: Intellectual Property and Security
sections.content:
Section 10 sets the rules for intellectual property rights. No contribution that is under a confidentiality requirement may be considered. By submitting a contribution, a contributor grants the Internet Society and the IETF a license to copy, publish and distribute it and to prepare derivative works, and represents that known proprietary rights have been disclosed.

If patent or other rights in a standards-track specification are known and brought to the IESG's attention, the IESG must not advance it without a note in the document about them. The IETF Executive Director tries to obtain a written assurance that any party can implement the technology under reasonable, non-discriminatory terms. The IESG does not judge the validity or scope of claimed rights. Standards-track documents must carry set notices, including an invitation to disclose rights.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: If someone owns a special part of an idea, they have to say so, and they should let others use it on fair terms. The rulebook itself says nothing about computer security.

items.label: Proposed Standard
items.desc: Entry level; stable and reviewed, but treated as immature.

items.label: Draft Standard
items.desc: At least two independent, interoperable implementations.

items.label: Internet Standard
items.desc: Significant implementation and operational experience; gets an STD number.

items.label: Experimental
items.desc: Part of a research or development effort.

items.label: Informational
items.desc: Published for general information; no community consensus implied.

items.title: Internet-Draft
items.text: At least two weeks before action can be recommended.

items.title: Last-Call
items.text: At least two weeks, or four if not from a working group.

items.title: Proposed Standard
items.text: At least six months at this level.

items.title: Draft Standard
items.text: At least four months, or until an IETF meeting, whichever is later.

items.title: Appeals
items.text: Must begin within two months of the action becoming public.
